name: The Schillereiche

location.address: Schillerhoehe lookout, Wernhaldenstrasse above Neue Weinsteige, Stuttgart

access: Free, open lookout with benches and a footpath beside Wernhaldenstrasse; the ground belongs to the Verschoenerungsverein Stuttgart, which keeps it as a public viewpoint. No ticket.
transport: Stadtbahn U5/U6 to Weinsteige, then roughly 10 to 15 minutes' walk along Wernhaldenstrasse (walk time estimated, not sourced)
verify_notes: Planted 1865 by the Verschoenerungsverein (VSV, owner of the plot, fetched 2026-10-18: 'Aussichtsanlage mit Eiche, 1865 errichtet und gepflanzt', planted in memory of the first reading from Schiller's Die Raeuber; Stuttgarter Zeitung per search summary gives the same year but is vague on where the reading happened, so treat the Raeuber link as the club's own account). Documented planting of THIS tree, so age derived at about 160 years (2026 minus 1865). Lookout on the Schillerhoehe, 408 m, view south-west to north-east over the city; a Kurhaus/restaurant Schillereiche once stood beside it and is gone; lookout renovated 2005 for the 200th anniversary of Schiller's death, with Garten-, Friedhofs- und Forstamt. No girth or height in any source found. ALIVE: Commons photo by Fyrtaarn dated 2024-05-05 shows a full-crowned oak in leaf on a path with a bench (viewed). PIN: that photo is geotagged 48.7625 9.181944, 4.5 m from the register coordinate (48.762458 9.181948): confirmed. PHOTO CANDIDATE (not downloaded into the repo): Commons 'Schillereiche (Wernhaldenstrasse, Stuttgart), 2024-05-05, yj.jpg', CC BY-SA 4.0, author Fyrtaarn, good Cadiz-standard framing, trunk and crown. Also 'Naturdenkmal Schillereiche, Stuttgart.jpg' (not examined). Same walk as stu_009 (about 250 m east).
story:
This oak was planted for a play. In 1865 the Verschönerungsverein, Stuttgart's beautification society, laid out a lookout on the Schillerhöhe and put this tree on it. By the club's own account it marks the first reading of Schiller's Die Räuber; a newspaper agrees on the year but is vaguer about where that reading happened, so treat the link to the play as the club's story.

The planting is what makes it datable, which is rarer than it sounds. Counted from 1865 rather than guessed from a trunk, it is about 160 years old. Nobody has published its girth or height.

It has outlasted most of what was built around it. A Kurhaus and restaurant named after the oak once stood beside it and is gone. In 2005, for the 200th anniversary of Schiller's death, the lookout was renovated together with the city's parks, cemeteries and forestry office. The club still owns the ground and keeps it open as a public viewpoint, and Stuttgart has protected the oak as a natural monument since 2003.

The view is the other reason to climb up. From 408 metres the lookout takes in the city from south-west to north-east, with benches beside the trunk and a footpath along Wernhaldenstraße. A photograph from May 2024 shows the crown full and in leaf.

Pair it with the Wernhalde sequoias, about 250 metres east on the same slope.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the oak on the Schillerhöhe lookout, with benches beside it and the city laid out below from 408 metres. It stands by the footpath along Wernhaldenstraße.

name: The Wernhalde Giant Sequoias

location.address: Steinkopfstrasse 6 and 8, beside the Wernhaldenpark, Stuttgart

access: View-only from the public street and footpath beside Steinkopfstrasse (visible over a fence in the Commons photo); the tree itself stands between houses and its plot status is not stated by any source. The Wernhaldenpark next door is public, with five entrances, steep paths and many more sequoias.
transport: Stadtbahn U5/U6 to Weinsteige, then about 10 minutes down Roemerstrasse into the park (per stuttgartwege blog route; time estimated)

Register is the only per-tree source; no girth or height found. Context (stuttgartwege blog, fetched): many of Stuttgart's and Wuerttemberg's sequoias trace to King Wilhelm I of Wuerttemberg, who bought a pound of seed in 1864; the park's sequoias have reached sizes 'unbelievable for Wuerttemberg'; a young planting of 1990 stands in the park (do not confuse). Planting date of these two ND trees is NOT documented: do not bridge the 1864 seed to them. Stuttgarter Nachrichten (search summary only, not used) says sequoias in the park are over 30 m. ALIVE: Commons photo by Laserlicht, 2018-04-06 (CC BY-SA 4.0, Wiki Loves Earth), viewed: a tall healthy conifer of about 35 m by eye behind a roadside rail, houses beside it. Pin stays approximate (register coordinate, not on a visible crown). Flagged: register only, access view-only, photo is the 2018 one. PHOTO CANDIDATE: that file, CC BY-SA 4.0, author Laserlicht, tree fills the frame vertically, daylight, bare trees around, passable. Neighbours not folded in: Bopserwaldstr. 79 copper beech (81110000408, 48.7647 9.18562) and Bopserwaldstr. 81 sequoia (81110000409, 48.76445 9.18555), residential street, unverified.
story:
Two giant sequoias stand about ten metres apart between the houses of Steinkopfstraße, and Stuttgart protects each one under its own number. The trees at number 6 and number 8 were made natural monuments in June 2003; we list them as one stop, because you will see them together.

Sequoias are something of a Stuttgart habit. A local walking writer traces many of the ones in the city and across Württemberg to King Wilhelm I, who bought a pound of seed in 1864, and describes the sequoias in the Wernhaldenpark next door as reaching sizes unbelievable for Württemberg. Whether these two grew from that pound of seed, nobody has recorded. Their planting date is not documented, and we are not going to borrow the king's year for them. If you know when they went in, tell us.

The official register is the only source that names these two individually, and it gives no girth or height. A photograph from April 2018 shows a tall, healthy conifer behind a roadside rail, with houses beside it.

Be clear about access. They stand between houses on ground no source describes, so these are trees to look at from the street and footpath, not to walk up to, and the pin is the register's approximate point. For sequoias you can stand under, the public Wernhaldenpark next door has many more on its steep paths, along with a young planting from 1990 not to be mistaken for the old ones.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the two giant sequoias about ten metres apart between the houses at Steinkopfstraße 6 and 8. You see them from the street over a fence, beside the Wernhaldenpark.

name: The Jahneiche

location.address: Marconistrasse at the end of Lange Allee, Zuffenhausen, Stuttgart

access: Standing at the junction of Lange Allee and Marconistrasse, a public street junction; no ticket. Exact surroundings (verge or green strip) not confirmed.

story:
By 1711 this oak was already called a stately old tree, and a duke chose it as the spot for his hunting lodge. That is the account in the German Wikipedia: Duke Eberhard Ludwig of Württemberg had a hunting pavilion built beside it for his Schlotwiese hunting ground. We have not seen the 1711 record behind the claim, so we carry it as Wikipedia's and put the tree's age no closer than over 300 years. Nobody has measured the trunk to test that. If the 1711 mention holds, it is the oldest tree on this page.

The name is far younger than the tree. In 1929 the Turnverein Zuffenhausen, the district's gymnastics club, marked its 40th anniversary by naming the oak after Friedrich Ludwig Jahn, the Turnvater of German gymnastics. A tree that stood in a duke's hunting ground now carries a gymnastics club's birthday present.

It has not had an untroubled old age. Some years ago, a local newspaper reported, a gust of wind broke off a heavy branch and the area around it was cordoned off. The report is no longer online. Stuttgart has protected the oak as a natural monument since 2003, and a photograph from April 2020 names it.

It stands where Lange Allee ends at Marconistraße. The pin is the register's approximate point, and no source describes whether the trunk sits on a verge or a green strip. If you go, tell us what you find, and its girth if you can measure it.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the old oak at the junction where Lange Allee ends at Marconistraße in Zuffenhausen. Another protected oak stands about 70 metres north-east; this is the one on the junction.

name: Franziska-Platane (Liebesplatane) at the Spielhaus, Hohenheim

name: The Wilhelma sequoia grove (Mammutbaumwaeldchen)

location.address: Wilhelma 13, Zoologisch-Botanischer Garten, Neckarvorstadt, Bad Cannstatt, Stuttgart (grove behind the main entrance)

access: Paid entry: inside the Wilhelma zoo and botanic garden (owner and manager of the ground); ticket price and hours not fetched this pass, check wilhelma.de. One sequoia at the grove's edge has a circular wooden platform (built 2023) so visitors can walk around and touch the trunk; the other trees are not approached, to protect roots.
transport: Wilhelma, Bad Cannstatt; nearest stop not checked this pass.
story:
A king asked for a little seed and got a pound of it. In 1864 King Wilhelm I of Württemberg ordered giant sequoia seed from America. As the Wilhelma tells it, he asked for a lot, meaning a small lot of about 15 grams, and the Americans sent a pound. The seedlings went out to parks and woods across the kingdom, and the Wilhelma counts this grove as where that seed's story starts. Germany's largest sequoia, 57 metres tall in the Rems-Murr district, grew from the same seed.

The grove behind the main entrance holds about 70 trees, which the garden puts at about 160 years old. Its tallest measures 38.6 metres by the Wilhelma's own figure. Local newspapers have printed other numbers over the years: a tallest of 37 metres, a thickest trunk of 4.2 or 4.7 metres round, fewer trees. We carry the garden's figures and leave the girth open.

The grove has not had an easy recent run. Climate change and drought have stressed it, and the Wilhelma has laid water lines and hydrants, aerated the soil and buried moisture sensors at four depths, saying the trees do not develop optimally.

Since 2023 one sequoia at the edge of the grove has a circular wooden platform round it, so you can walk all the way round and put a hand on the bark. The rest are left alone to protect their roots. Entry is paid, and the pin marks the garden rather than the grove.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise the one to visit by the circular wooden platform round its trunk, at the edge of a grove of about 70 giant sequoias. The grove stands behind the Wilhelma's main entrance.
verify_notes: Ensemble with one place to stand (the platform tree at the grove edge). Pin is the Wilhelma garden centre (Nominatim relation 13371824 centre 48.80585 9.20467), NOT the grove: no source gave a grove coordinate; treat as park-level approximate. Wilhelma's own press release 31.03.2023 (fetched 2026-10-20): the Mammutbaumwaeldchen has about 70 trees, the tallest 38.6 m, trees are about 160 years old, seed was ordered by King Wilhelm I of Wuerttemberg in 1864 from America (the legend: he ordered a 'lot', about 15 g, and the Americans delivered 'a lot', a pound of seed); the seedlings were planted in many parks and woods of the kingdom, so this is the origin place of the Wilhelma-Saat sequoias; the largest sequoia in Germany (57 m, Rems-Murr-Kreis, from the same seed) is named there. Stress: climate change and drought; Wilhelma laid water lines, hydrants and soil aeration and installed soil-moisture sensors at four depths, saying the trees 'do not develop optimally'. Conflicts, seen only as search-result text of the Stuttgarter Zeitung and Stuttgarter Nachrichten (articles not fetched this pass; earlier lead notes record: StZ 2016 almost sixty trees, tallest 37 m, girth 4.20 m; StN 4.7 m girth for the thickest, 35 original trees now about 70): tallest 37 m versus 38.6 m (owner's figure wins), girth 4.20 m versus 4.7 m (probably different trees); girth_cm left empty because no fetched page has it. Seeds sown under glass 1865 per an info board quoted in search results (not fetched). Single source for most figures (the owner of the ground, which is enough per rulebook). Alive: press release 2023 says the grove stands; lifecheck not run (no tree coordinate). Not the Rosensteinpark sequoias.

name: The Wilhelma Ginkgo

location.address: Wilhelma Zoologisch-Botanischer Garten, beside the Palmenhaus near the main entrance, Bad Cannstatt, Stuttgart

official_register.name: Deutsche Dendrologische Gesellschaft champion tree list (Rekordbaeume), ID 3801, rank DE 15 and BW 4 for Ginkgo

access: Paid entry: inside the Wilhelma zoo and botanic garden; DDG record states 'oeffentlich zugaenglich, Oeffnungszeiten beachten, Eintrittsgeld'. Ticket price and hours not fetched this pass, check wilhelma.de.
transport: Wilhelma, Bad Cannstatt; nearest stop not checked this pass.
story:
Two male ginkgos stand side by side at the Wilhelma's Palmenhaus, and the eastern one is the fourth-largest of its kind in Baden-Württemberg. That ranking comes from the German Dendrological Society's champion-tree list, which also puts it 15th in Germany. In August 2019 Jürgen Blümle measured its trunk at 4.58 metres round at chest height.

Its age is an estimate, and the record is honest about how loose it is. It gives about 167 years, planted around 1859, then notes that it may have gone in as early as 1840. Neither date is documented for this tree, so we carry it as somewhere between about 160 and 190 years. If you know when it was planted, tell us.

What the record is sure of is its health. When it was measured in 2019 the tree was judged fully vital, its wood undamaged.

Being male has a practical upside. Female ginkgos drop fleshy seeds in autumn that smell strongly; this pair does not. What both do is turn, usually in November, the whole crown going butter gold before the leaves come down within a day or two. That is the week to go.

Entry to the Wilhelma is paid and runs to opening hours, so check before you set out. Inside, find the Palmenhaus near the main entrance and the two ginkgos beside it, and take the one on the east.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the eastern of the two male ginkgos standing side by side, its trunk 4.58 metres round at chest height. It stands beside the Palmenhaus near the Wilhelma's main entrance.

best_time.label: November, when the whole crown turns butter gold and drops within days

verify_notes: DDG champion-tree record (fetched 2026-10-20): Ginkgo biloba, 'Wilhelma, am Palmenhaus Naehe Haupteingang', girth 458 cm at 1.3 m, measured August 2019 by Juergen Bluemle (reported by Volker Andre Bouffier), age 'ca. 167 Jahre (geschaetzt ca. 1859)', note 'Oestlicher Baum der beiden maennlichen Ginkgos, Pflanzung evtl. schon 1840', vitality 'vollkommen vital', wood body 'keine Schaeden', GPS 48.804984, 9.207091 (published GPS, so pin confirmed; note two male ginkgos stand side by side, this one is the eastern of the pair). Rank DE 15 and BW 4 among ginkgos in the DDG list. Source for the data: Beitraege zur Gehoelzkunde 2013 pp. 211-261 and Bluemle, Baumschaetze Baden-Wuerttembergs, 2nd ed. 2023 (not seen). monumentaltrees.com (cross-check only, same measurer, not independent, not fetched because the host 403s; figures known from search result text): 4.40 m girth measured 10 Oct 2010, planted about 1840 +/- 10; the 2010 to 2019 growth from 440 to 458 cm is plausible. Age is an estimate with planting date uncertain (1840 or 1859), never documented for this specimen: kept broad. Both measurements come from one person, so independence is weak; the ground's owner (Wilhelma) is the access source. Life check: lifecheck.py at the pin returned RECENT 2026-04-30 (iNaturalist observation 357703226, not opened); DDG itself records full vitality in 2019. No photo hunted (DDG pictures by Bluemle are (c) with rights page, not usable without checking).
